notes.meaning: A father warns his son about making a hasty promise to back another person's debt. Shaking hands on an agreement like this can trap a person in obligations they cannot manage. A promise made without careful thought can quickly bring financial ruin. We must always think carefully before guaranteeing what someone else owes.

A person who gets caught in such a pledge needs to act right away. The teacher says to swallow your pride, go straight to the person you backed, and beg them to handle the debt. It is far better to humble yourself than to lose your home or freedom.

There is no time to delay or sleep when your future is at stake. You should fight to get free just like a deer breaks away from a hunter or a bird flies out of a trap. Escaping a dangerous financial trap demands total effort and speed.

The teacher tells lazy people to look closely at the tiny ant and learn how to live. Ants have no boss, officer, or ruler standing over them to make them work. Yet they work hard during the summer and harvest to gather food for the days ahead. Wise people do what needs to be done without waiting to be told.

The teacher asks the lazy person how long they plan to stay in bed. Wasting daylight while life passes by is foolish and harmful. It is a direct call to wake up, get moving, and take care of daily duties.

The lazy person only asks for a little more sleep and just a few more moments of rest. But those small delays pile up until extreme poverty arrives suddenly, like a bandit attacking by surprise. A habit of putting off hard work leaves a person defenseless when real need strikes.

A truly wicked person uses dishonest words and sneaky body language to deceive others. Such a person winks, taps their feet, and points to pass secret signals while pretending to be harmless. Inwardly, their heart is always planning trouble and stirring up fights among neighbors.

Ruin will strike such a troublemaker without any warning. Like a clay pot smashed to pieces, that person will be shattered completely and cannot be repaired. Those who plot harm against others bring sudden disaster upon themselves.

The writer uses a counting pattern to catch our attention and highlight a special list. Saying there are six things, even seven, builds up toward the worst evil of all. These are sins the Lord deeply detests because they ruin peace and destroy human lives.

The list starts with proud looks, lying tongues, and hands that kill innocent people. It goes on to hearts that plan evil, feet eager to do wrong, witnesses who lie in court, and anyone who stirs up fights among brothers. God especially despises people who break apart families and communities with their malice.

Children are urged to hold firmly to the godly lessons their father and mother taught them. Treasuring these instructions is like tying a precious jewel around your neck and locking it in your heart. Keeping God's truth close guards our thoughts and guides our choices every day.

God's teaching acts like a faithful friend who guides your steps, protects your sleep, and speaks to your mind when you wake. His commands shine like a lamp along a dark trail, showing the safe path to take. Loving discipline and correction keep us from walking into danger.

Treasuring God's word protects a young man from the seductive words and flattering talk of an immoral woman. He is warned not to feed lust in his heart or let her beautiful glances capture his attention. Guarding the eyes and the mind is the first step in staying sexually pure.

Going after an unfaithful woman comes at a terrible price. Chasing a prostitute can leave a man with nothing but a crust of bread, while sleeping with another man's wife risks his very life. Sin promises pleasure but takes away a person's future and freedom.

No one can carry hot coals in their lap without setting their clothes on fire, or walk on burning embers without scorching their feet. In the same way, anyone who sleeps with another man's wife cannot escape painful punishment. Sin brings natural and unavoidable consequences, just like walking into fire.

People do not completely hate a starving person who steals food just to survive, even though they still pity him. Yet even that hungry thief must pay back everything he stole, perhaps giving up all the wealth in his house. Restitution can settle the thief's debt, but some crimes cannot be repaid with money.

A man who commits adultery lacks basic good sense and destroys his own life. Instead of satisfying a real need, he brings permanent shame, physical injury, and a ruined reputation upon himself. Adultery leaves a stain on a person's name that is never forgotten.

An injured husband burns with fierce jealousy and will not show mercy when he takes revenge. No amount of money, bribes, or lavish gifts will soothe his anger or convince him to drop the matter. Breaking apart a marriage unleashes a fury that cannot be bought off.
